# Ezekiel 32: Research notes

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Constable dates this to March 3, 585 B.C., less than two months after the exiles heard Jerusalem had fallen. In his reading, the message told both the exiles and the Egyptians that God would bring Egypt down. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Guzik adds that it came after any hope that Egypt would help Judah had passed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-32/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown counts the twelfth year from Jehoiachin's exile. By then Jerusalem had fallen and Amasis was starting his revolt against Pharaoh Hophra. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/32-1.htm
- Ellicott (on the same page) splits the chapter in two: a lament over Pharaoh (vv. 1–16) and a funeral song for his burial with his multitude (vv. 17–32). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/32-1.htm

**v. 2:** Constable says Hophra saw himself as a young lion but was really more like the mythical sea monster, probably a crocodile. Muddying the Nile pictures how Pharaoh disrupted the world scene and complicated God's dealings with Judah and Babylon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Keil & Delitzsch say the picture is a crocodile breaking out into the streams and stirring up mud with its feet. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-32.html
- Matthew Henry draws a lesson for ministers: they should lament the ruin of sinners, showing they are moved by it themselves. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_032.cfm
- Kingcomments calls Pharaoh a cruel ruler and an unreliable ally. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/ezekiel-32.html

**v. 3:** Kingcomments says God's net is Babylon and the nations with it, tools in His hand. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/ezekiel-32.html
- Constable compares the Babylonian creation story, where the god Marduk catches the chaos monster Tiamat in a net. Because Egyptians saw Pharaoh, the crocodile and the Nile as signs of their gods, he takes the verse to mean God would humble Egypt's gods too. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html

**vv. 4–6:** Constable says Pharaoh is put on dry land, out of his element, and eaten by birds and beasts. He reads this as a picture of Egyptians scattered from their land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Guzik quotes Poole: this was literally fulfilled in the Libyan deserts, where Hophra's dead soldiers were left for birds and beasts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-32/
- Guzik links the blood in v. 6 to the first plague (Exodus 7:19). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-32/
- The Pulpit Commentary asks whether Ezekiel had that plague in mind and calls the flood of blood a symbol of the invaders who would overrun Egypt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/32.htm
- Matthew Henry takes it as so many dead soldiers that bodies lie across the hills and blood swells the rivers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_032.cfm
- Ellicott says the "land wherein thou swimmest" (v. 6) probably means the land the Nile floods, now soaked with blood. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/32.htm

**vv. 7–8:** Ellicott says v. 7 closely follows Isaiah 13:10, a prophecy about Babylon, and uses the common prophetic picture of changes in the heavens for God's judgments. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/32-7.htm
- Gill and Clarke read it as a code: heaven is the kingdom, the sun the king, the moon the queen and the stars the nobles. Gill says the verse pictures a kingdom's collapse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/32-7.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/32-7.html
- Keil & Delitzsch say this is more than a picture of mourning. The image rests on the day of the Lord, which breaks over Egypt when Pharaoh falls. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/32-7.htm
- Constable and Guzik both link it to the plague of darkness (Exodus 10). Constable says God would again humble the gods Egypt credited with light. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-32/
- Kingcomments says Pharaoh, who acted like a sun god, will be put out. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/ezekiel-32.html

**vv. 9–10:** Keil & Delitzsch say these verses are about the fear God sends on the nations, not their mourning. The Hebrew word means to fill the heart with anxiety and take away its peace. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-32.html
- Constable: other kings would fear for their own safety. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Guzik: they saw that if judgment could fall on Egypt, it could fall on them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-32/

**vv. 11–12:** Constable: God sends Babylon's army against Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Guzik quotes Feinberg against skeptics who doubt Nebuchadnezzar conquered Egypt. Feinberg says Herodotus saying nothing about it proves little. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-32/

**vv. 13–14:** Constable says Egyptians saw many kinds of cattle as signs of their gods. The still, oil-smooth waters mean no one is left to stir them up. He says some take this as the messianic age, but it probably doesn't look that far ahead. He also cites Block: rivers of oil usually picture paradise-like peace in biblical and Jewish tradition. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Guzik quotes Wiersbe: with no people or animals to work the land, the water would flow smoothly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-32/

**v. 15:** Constable: God again humbles Egypt's gods and shows He is in charge, as at the Exodus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- He also quotes Cooper: "know that I am the LORD" occurs 19 times in these oracles, and the main aim is that everyone should know the LORD. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html

**v. 16:** Constable: other nations would chant this lament, like hired mourning women at a funeral. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Guzik quotes Poole: it is a funeral speech recalling Egypt's old glory and its present shame. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-32/
- Smith says the first lament ends here, and v. 17 starts a new prophecy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/ezekiel-32.html

**v. 17:** Constable dates it about two weeks later, March 18, 585 B.C. He notes it uses a different rhythm (2+2) from the usual funeral lament (3+2). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Guzik says most assume it is the same month, and it is the last of seven prophecies against Egypt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-32/

**v. 18:** Kingcomments: Ezekiel's words bring death to Egypt because they are the LORD's words. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/ezekiel-32.html
- Gill and Poole say Egypt's kings expected grand tombs but would be buried in common pits with ordinary people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/32-18.htm
- Cambridge (same page) argues the "daughters of famous nations" are the ones doing the burying, not the ones buried. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/32-18.htm

**v. 19:** Constable: Egypt's beauty wins no special treatment; she lies with the peoples she looked down on. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Guzik quotes Clarke that a well-embalmed mummy is no better than any other corpse. He also quotes Poole: Egypt practised circumcision, but burial with the uncircumcised was a mark of dishonour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-32/
- Dummelow reads "uncircumcised" as dishonourably buried. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-32.html

**vv. 20–21:** Constable: dead nations describe Egypt's end as that of an uncircumcised people like themselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Guzik quotes Block: the greeting is a harsh taunt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-32/
- Barnes says "uncircumcised" throughout means pagans seen as impure. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/32-21.htm

**vv. 22–23:** Bible.org (Utley) says "remotest parts of the pit" is an idiom for the worst or lowest places. They were killed in this world and humiliated in the next. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21727
- Constable: Assyria once terrified others and now lies in the grave. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html

**vv. 24–25:** Constable: Elam was destroyed by Ashurbanipal around 645 B.C. Neither Assyria nor Elam practised circumcision, yet circumcised Egypt joins them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says their "shame" is being uncircumcised and so placed in the lower circles of the dead. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-32.html

**v. 26:** Guzik reports interpreters disagree on who Meshech and Tubal were: remnants of the Hittites or the Scythians. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-32/
- Constable places them in eastern Anatolia. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Matthew Henry treats them as Scythians. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_032.cfm

**v. 27:** Constable: some countries buried honoured warriors with their weapons, and he compares the legendary warriors of Genesis 6:4. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Gill, following the KJV wording "their iniquities shall be upon their bones," says the Scythians get no honoured burial, and their punishment is bones left unburied. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/32-27.html
- Barnes: their sins followed them to the grave. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/32-27.htm
- Ellicott: they die in their sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/32-27.htm

**v. 28:** Trapp says Pharaoh will suffer a deeper torment in hell. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/ezekiel-32.html
- Matthew Henry: when God brings down nations that won't humble themselves, Egypt must expect to fall with them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_032.cfm

**v. 29:** Constable: Edom, once strong, joins everyone else in the grave. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Matthew Henry notes the Edomites kept circumcision because they descended from Abraham. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/32-27.html

**v. 30:** Constable says "princes of the north" may mean Phoenician coastal towns including Tyre, or invaders from between the Black and Caspian Seas. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Matthew Henry: these sea peoples are now ashamed of the strength they boasted in. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_032.cfm

**vv. 31–32:** Constable says Pharaoh takes some comfort in not suffering alone. Egyptians thought their burial customs guaranteed safe passage after death, but their rest would be the same as everyone's. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Gill: seeing other kings in the same state comforts Pharaoh a little. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/32-31.html
- Matthew Henry quotes Greenhill: the comfort of the wicked after death is imaginary, not real. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_032.cfm
- Bible Hub's summary disagrees and says Pharaoh finds no comfort. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/32.htm
- Trapp: "my terror" refers to Pharaoh's punishment, made an example to others. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/ezekiel-32.html

## 2. Where readings differ

I found no denominational sources, so I can't sort these by tradition. The differences below are between individual commentators.

**vv. 17–32 (what Sheol is like):**
- Guzik, citing Block, says the dead in Sheol are fully conscious and aware of each other. He calls the passage an Old Testament glimpse of conscious life after death, though poetic. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-32/
- Trapp calls the deaths "a trap door to eternal torment" (quoted by Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-32/
- Constable, quoting Taylor, says this is not the chapter to turn to for the Bible's teaching on the afterlife. He also quotes Block calling it a "literary cartoon" rather than a photograph. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Dummelow sees two levels: Sheol for heroes given honourable burial, and the pit for violent nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-32.html

**vv. 7–8 (does this point to the end times?):**
- Smith suggests a double fulfilment: Nebuchadnezzar's conquest and also the Great Tribulation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/csc/ezekiel-32.html
- Constable quotes Feinberg that Egypt's fall previewed the end of world rule in the last days. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-32.html
- Bible Hub's notes treat the signs as literal and as pointing ahead to end-times events. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/32-7.htm
- The older writers Gill and Clarke read the same signs as symbols of a kingdom falling. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/32-7.htm

**v. 27 (two ways to read the Hebrew):**
- Some translations read "shields on their bones": the BSB, and the NET Bible as shown in Bible Hub's parallel texts. https://biblehub.com/lexicon/ezekiel/32-27.htm
- The KJV, ESV and NASB read "iniquities" or "punishment" on their bones. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/32-27.htm
- Cambridge (on Bible Hub) calls the "shields" guess highly improbable. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/32-27.htm
- There is also a question whether the honoured warriors rest in a better place than Meshech and Tubal. Cambridge rejects that idea. Keil & Delitzsch (citing à Lapide) accept it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/32-27.htm

## 3. Other views
I found nothing from the modern-scholarship, Catholic or Orthodox sites. I also found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching for this chapter.
